B1C1: Defines the wise man's twofold office: to meditate and teach divine truth, and to refute the errors opposed to it, following Wisdom's own words in Proverbs.
B1C2: States Aquinas's purpose: to declare Catholic truth by natural reason as far as possible, since pursuing wisdom is the noblest, most delightful, and most God-like human activity.
B1C3: Distinguishes two kinds of divine truth: those demonstrable by natural reason (God exists, is one) and those wholly surpassing reason (the Trinity), each requiring a different mode of proof.
B1C4: Explains why truths about God attainable by reason are still fittingly proposed as objects of faith, since few people would otherwise ever come to know them with certainty.
B1C5: Argues that truths exceeding reason are fittingly given as objects of faith so man's mind is drawn to aspire beyond the present life toward a higher, supernatural good.
B1C6: Defends belief in truths above reason as reasonable rather than foolish, since miracles and the Holy Spirit's inspiration of the unlearned confirm the divine origin of the faith.
B1C7: Argues that reason's naturally known truths cannot contradict the truths of faith, since both ultimately derive from the same, non-deceiving God.
B1C8: Continues showing reason's inability to fully refute faith, noting that even imperfect natural knowledge of divine things is precious and that seeming rational objections to faith are not true demonstrations.
B1C9: Outlines the treatise's method: using demonstrative arguments for truths reason can prove, and using arguments from fittingness and refutation of objections for truths that surpass reason.
B1C10: Examines and sets up for refutation the Anselmian-style view that God's existence is self-evident and therefore not something that needs, or can be, demonstrated.
B1C11: Refutes the claim that God's existence is self-evident to us, distinguishing what is self-evident in itself from what is self-evident only to those who grasp the divine essence, which we do not.
B1C12: Rejects the opposite extreme, the fideist view that God's existence can be known only by faith, arguing that natural reason truly can demonstrate that God exists.
B1C14: Introduces the method of remotion (negative theology) as the chief way to investigate the divine essence, since God's immensity surpasses every concept our intellect can form.
B1C15: Proves that God is eternal, having neither beginning nor end, since He is wholly unchangeable and unmeasured by time, which requires movement.
B1C16: Proves there is no passive potentiality in God, since He is eternal, the first cause, and pure actuality with nothing prior to bring Him into act.
B1C17: Proves God is not matter, since matter is potential and not a principle of activity, whereas God is the first efficient cause and wholly immovable.
B1C18: Proves there is no composition in God, since every composite requires act and potentiality united, parts prior to the whole, and dissolubility, none of which fit the first simple being.
B1C19: Proves nothing in God is violent or contrary to His nature, since simplicity precludes anything added, and God is necessary of Himself, not compelled by another.
B1C20: Proves God is not a body, since every body is composite, quantitatively divisible and potential, and, if physical, would be movable — all incompatible with God's simplicity and pure actuality.
B1C21: Proves God is His own essence, quiddity, or nature, since any distinction between a thing and its essence would introduce composition, which is impossible in God.
B1C22: Proves that in God essence and existence are identical, since God's necessary being cannot be separate from, or added to, what He is.
B1C23: Proves no accident can be in God, since His existence is His substance and cannot receive anything additional without a cause, which would compromise His status as first cause.
B1C24: Proves the divine being cannot be specified by an added substantial difference the way a genus is divided into species, since God's being is already the fullness of being itself.
B1C25: Proves God is not contained in any genus, since a genus requires specific differences and potentiality, whereas God is subsistent being itself with no addition.
B1C26: Refutes the view that God is merely the common formal being of all things, since divine being is neither substantial nor accidental being shared univocally by creatures.
B1C27: Proves God is not the form of any body or thing, since form is a principle of being rather than being itself, and union with matter would introduce composition and potentiality.
B1C28: Explains the divine perfection: God, being identical with His own existence, is universally perfect, lacking no excellence found dispersed among all other beings.
B1C29: Explains how creatures can be like God despite the infinite distance between them: as effects bear an imperfect, analogous likeness to a transcendent equivocal cause, as heat resembles the sun.
B1C30: Discusses which terms can be predicated of God: absolute perfections like goodness and wisdom apply properly, while terms bound to a creaturely mode of being apply only metaphorically.
B1C31: Shows that God's perfection and the many names applied to Him do not compromise His simplicity, since our many concepts reflect our limited way of knowing one simple reality.
B1C32: Proves that nothing is predicated univocally of God and creatures, since creaturely forms only partially and diversely receive what exists in God simply and universally.
B1C33: Proves that terms applied to God and creatures are not purely equivocal either, since there remains an ordered relationship of cause and effect between them, unlike accidental equivocation.
B1C34: Concludes that terms applied to God and creatures are used analogically, by reference to one thing (God) as cause, rather than univocally or purely equivocally.
B1C35: Shows that the many names predicated of God, though signifying one simple reality, are not synonymous, since each conveys a distinct conception formed from a different creaturely perfection.
B1C36: Explains how the intellect can rightly form propositions about the simple God through composition and division, attributing the diversity to its own mode of understanding, not to God.
B1C37: Proves that God is good, since goodness follows upon perfection and being the object of all desire, both of which belong supremely to God as first mover and end.
B1C38: Proves God is goodness itself, not merely good by participation, since His perfection is His very essence rather than something added to it.
B1C39: Proves no evil can be in God, since God is essentially goodness itself, and evil, being contrary to goodness, cannot coexist with an essence that simply is goodness.
B1C40: Proves God is the good of every good, since His infinite perfection contains virtually all created perfections, which are good only by resemblance to Him.
B1C41: Proves God is the sovereign good, since the universal good surpasses every particular good, and all things derive their goodness from Him as from its supreme cause.
B1C42: Proves there is only one God, since the sovereign, absolutely perfect good and the best possible order of the universe both require unity of source and governance.
B1C43: Proves God is infinite, not in quantity, but in the spiritual magnitude of His power and the perfection of His nature, which is unlimited by any receiving matter or form.
B1C44: Proves God is intelligent, arguing that the first unmoved self-mover of all things must move by appetite and apprehension, and thus by intellect and will.
B1C45: Proves that God's act of intelligence is identical with His essence, since His understanding, like all that is in Him, cannot be really distinct from His being.
B1C46: Proves God understands solely through His own essence, not through any other intelligible species, since nothing can be prior to or cause the divine essence.
B1C47: Proves God understands Himself perfectly, since the intelligible species by which He understands — His own essence — is fully identical with and united to His intellect.
B1C48: Proves that God knows Himself first and per se as the primary object of His intellect, since His essence alone is the species by which He understands.
B1C49: Proves God knows things other than Himself, since knowing His essence as the cause of all things entails knowing the effects contained virtually within that cause.
B1C50: Proves God has proper, distinct knowledge of each individual thing, not merely a general knowledge of being, since He knows Himself as cause of every particular effect.
B1C51: Raises the difficulty of how the divine intellect can understand many distinct things without introducing multiplicity or composition into God's simple essence.
B1C52: Continues examining the problem of how multiple things understood by God are compatible with the unity and simplicity of the divine intellect, surveying inadequate solutions.
B1C53: Begins solving the difficulty by analyzing how understood things exist in any intellect through intelligible species that are likenesses of, though not identical with, their objects.
B1C54: Explains how God's one simple essence can serve as the proper likeness of many diverse things, since it possesses their perfections eminently and virtually, not by mere generic sameness.
B1C55: Proves God understands all things simultaneously in a single act, since His single intelligible species (His essence) suffices to represent every object of knowledge at once.
B1C56: Proves God's knowledge is not a habit but always fully actual, since habitual knowledge implies potentiality, while God knows all things actually and simultaneously.
B1C57: Proves God's knowledge is not discursive or argumentative, since He does not reason from premises to conclusions but grasps all truths at once in a single, simple act.
B1C58: Proves God does not understand by composing and dividing concepts as we do, since He knows His essence, which contains no composition, directly and as it is.
B1C59: Shows that despite not knowing by composition and division, God is not ignorant of the truth of propositions, since He knows perfectly what those compositions and divisions signify in reality.
B1C60: Proves that God is truth itself, since truth is a perfection of intellectual operation, and God's act of understanding is identical with His perfect, unparticipated substance.
B1C61: Proves God is the most pure truth, containing no admixture of falsehood or error, since His intellect never errs about what things are and is not discursive.
B1C62: Proves that the divine truth is the first and supreme truth, since truth follows being, and God's being is first, most perfect, and the cause of all created truth.
B1C63: Lays out seven arguments used by those who deny that God can know singular, individual things, based on singularity's dependence on matter and other objections.
B1C64: Announces the order of topics to be treated regarding divine knowledge: singulars, non-existents, future contingents, acts of will, infinites, trivial things, and evils.
B1C65: Proves God knows singular things, not merely universals, since His effects are always singular and He knows things according to the way He causes them to exist.
B1C66: Proves God knows things that do not actually exist, comparing His knowledge to a craftsman's, whose art knows in advance the particular works not yet produced.
B1C67: Proves God has unerring knowledge of future contingent events, since His eternal knowledge views all things as present, where contingency and certainty are compatible.
B1C68: Proves God knows the secret movements and thoughts of the human will, since He knows His essence as cause of everything, including all interior acts of intellect and will.
B1C69: Proves God knows infinite things, since His causal power and His perfect knowledge of His own infinite power extend to whatever might exist, including an infinite multitude.
B1C70: Proves God knows even the most trivial and lowly things, since the infinite power of His intellect, unlike finite created powers, is not limited in the range of its knowledge.
B1C71: Proves God knows evil things as well as good, since knowledge of a good's privation is included in perfect knowledge of that good, and God's knowledge is entirely perfect.
B1C72: Proves there is will in God, since willing follows from understanding good, and God, who perfectly understands the good, must therefore possess will.
B1C73: Proves God's will is identical with His essence, since to will, like to understand, is a perfection abiding within the agent, and God's every act is His very being.
B1C74: Proves the principal object of God's will is His own essence, since the good understood, chiefly His own goodness, is the primary object toward which His will is directed.
B1C75: Proves that in willing Himself as the last end, God also wills other things, since whoever wills an end wills the means that are ordered to it.
B1C76: Proves God wills Himself and all other things by a single act of His will, since His goodness, as the end, gives the formal aspect under which all else is willed.
B1C77: Shows that the plurality of things God wills does not compromise divine simplicity, since all willed things are unified in being ordered toward the one divine goodness.
B1C78: Proves that God's will extends to particular, individual goods and not merely to a general willing of goodness as such, since He is compared as cause even to singulars.
B1C79: Proves that God wills even things that do not yet exist, resolving the apparent difficulty that willing seems to require the coexistence of the wilier and the thing willed.
B1C80: Proves God necessarily wills His own being and goodness as His principal object, since He cannot will Himself not to exist without contradiction.
B1C81: Proves God does not necessarily will things other than Himself, since His goodness is complete without them and the will need not choose means when the end is already secured.
B1C82: Raises objections claiming that if God does not will creatures of absolute necessity, His will must be indeterminate, potential, and changeable, seemingly contrary to divine simplicity.
B1C83: Resolves the objections by distinguishing absolute necessity from necessity of supposition: once God's unchangeable will wills something, it is necessarily so by supposition, though not absolutely necessary.
B1C84: Proves God's will cannot be directed toward things that are impossible or self-contradictory in themselves, since willing such things would conflict with what He necessarily wills.
B1C85: Proves the divine will does not eliminate contingency or impose absolute necessity on creatures, since God wills each effect according to the mode, contingent or necessary, proper to its nature.
B1C86: Shows that a reason can be assigned for the divine will, namely the divine goodness as end, and the good of the whole universe as the reason particular goods are willed.
B1C87: Proves nothing can be the efficient cause of the divine will, though a reason can be given, since God's goodness alone is the cause and object of His willing.
B1C88: Proves free-will exists in God, since He wills things other than Himself not of necessity but according to the judgment of His intellect, as befits a rational wilier.
B1C89: Proves the passions of the sensitive appetite are not in God, since passions require bodily change and sense knowledge, both of which are incompatible with God's immateriality.
B1C90: Proves that delight and joy, unlike other passions, are compatible with divine perfection, since joy simply follows from possessing a present good, which God eternally possesses in Himself.
B1C91: Proves love is in God as an act of His will, since He truly wills good to Himself and to other things, which is the very nature of love.
B1C92: Explains how virtues, though normally acquired habits in us, are ascribed to God as identical with His essence rather than as distinct dispositions added to Him.
B1C93: Shows that the moral virtues concerned with action, such as justice, prudence, liberality, and truthfulness, are fittingly ascribed to God according to His perfect intellect and will.
B1C94: Shows that the contemplative virtues — wisdom, science, and understanding — belong most properly to God, who knows Himself and all causes and effects perfectly.
B1C95: Proves that God cannot will evil, since His will is His virtuous essence, and willing evil would require an error of judgment, which is impossible in the divine intellect.
B1C96: Proves that hatred cannot be ascribed to God, since as He wills good to everything through loving His own goodness reflected in creatures, He can hate nothing that exists.
B1C97: Proves God is a living being, since intelligence and will, which have been shown to exist in God, belong properly only to things that live.
B1C98: Proves God is His own life, not merely a living being possessing life as something added, since His act of understanding, identical with His existence, is itself His life.
B1C99: Proves God's life is eternal, since nothing can sever Him from His own life, being Himself His life, and His life, like His existence, has no cause that could end it.
B1C100: Proves God is happy, since happiness is the proper good of an intellectual nature already possessing, rather than merely seeking, its perfect operation and object.
B1C101: Proves God is His own happiness, since His happiness consists in His intellectual operation, which is identical with His substance and the object He principally wills.
B1C102: Concludes Book One by showing that God's happiness is uniquely perfect and surpasses all other happiness, since He alone is happiness itself rather than merely a possessor of it.
B2C1: Introduces Book Two by explaining that knowing a thing fully requires knowing its operation, so having considered God's inner life, Aquinas now turns to God's outward act of producing creatures.
B2C4: Distinguishes the philosopher's and the theologian's approaches to creatures: philosophy studies creatures in themselves, while faith considers them as reflections of and pointers toward God.
B2C5: Outlines the order of Book Two: first the production of things into being, then their distinction from one another, then the nature of these created things as pertains to faith.
B2C6: Proves it is fitting for God to be the source of being to other things, since He is the first efficient cause and first unmoved mover from which all other beings and movements derive.
B2C7: Proves active power is fittingly ascribed to God, since active power follows from being in act, and God, being pure act and source of being to others, must possess active power.
B2C8: Proves that God's power is identical with His substance, since God is pure act with no potentiality, and whatever is ascribed to Him cannot be by participation but must be His very being.
B2C9: Proves that God's power is not distinct from His action, since both are identical with His substance, and things identical with the same thing are identical with one another.
B2C10: Clarifies that power is ascribed to God properly in relation to the things He makes, not as a principle really distinct from His action, which differs from power only in our mode of understanding.
B2C11: Shows that things can rightly be said of God in relation to creatures, since power implies a relation to effects, and correlative terms about creatures' dependence on God imply a converse reference to Him.
B2C12: Proves that the relations said of God with reference to creatures are not real in God as accidents or as His substance, since neither would be compatible with His independence and simplicity.
B2C15: Proves that God is the cause of being to absolutely everything besides Himself, since nothing can be predicated of two distinct things without one being the cause of it in the other or a common cause existing.
B2C16: Proves that God brought things into being out of nothing, with no pre-existing matter, since positing prior matter would either require an infinite regress or presuppose God as its uncaused source.
B2C17: Proves that creation, properly speaking, is neither movement nor change, since it presupposes no pre-existing potentiality or subject undergoing transformation.
B2C18: Answers objections against creation drawn from the nature of ordinary change, explaining that creation is really the creature's relation of dependence on its cause, not a transmutation.
B2C19: Proves that creation involves no succession or process, since succession belongs to movement, and there is no intermediate state between non-being and being for a thing to pass through.
B2C20: Proves that no body can create anything, since bodily action requires motion and succession, whereas creation, being instantaneous and without succession, is beyond any bodily agent's power.
B2C21: Proves that creation is an action proper to God alone, since it is the first and most excellent action, presupposing nothing else, fitting only the first and most excellent agent.
B2C23: Proves that God does not act by necessity of nature in producing creatures but by the free judgment of His will, since His power and effects are not confined to a single determined outcome.
B2C24: Proves that God produces His effects according to His wisdom, since His will, moved by His intellectual apprehension of Himself, acts as a voluntary and hence wise agent.
B2C25: Explains in what sense the almighty God is said to be unable to do certain things, namely those requiring passive potentiality, which cannot exist in God who is purely actual.
B2C26: Proves the divine intellect is not confined to knowing only certain determined effects, since it comprehends all things that can proceed from God by understanding His own essence.
B2C27: Proves the divine will is not confined to producing only certain determinate effects, since the will is proportioned to the intellect's unlimited grasp of possible goods and acts by free ordinance, not necessity.
B2C30: Explains how absolute necessity can still exist among created things despite their dependence on God's free will, since some creatures by their nature admit no potentiality to non-being.
B2C31: Proves it is not necessary that creatures have existed from eternity, since neither the universe nor any creature possesses of itself or from another an absolute necessity to always have been.
B2C34: Presents philosophical arguments for the eternity of the world drawn from considerations about how things come to be made, including the common maxim that nothing is made from nothing.
B2C35: Begins refuting arguments for the world's eternity taken from God's side, showing that a new effect need not imply change or a new action in the unchanging, eternal God.
B2C36: Continues refuting arguments for the world's eternity, this time those drawn from the nature of creatures themselves, distinguishing a necessity of order from an absolute necessity to have always existed.
B2C37: Refutes the arguments for the world's eternity based on the making of things, clarifying that the philosophers' maxim about nothing coming from nothing applies only to particular, not universal, causation.
B2C38: Presents arguments used by some to prove the world was not eternal, including the impossibility of an infinite regress of past days and of a cause not preceding its effect in duration.
B2C39: Proves that the diversity and distinction among created things is not the result of mere chance, since some things, like immaterial substances, exist by necessity and cannot arise by chance.
B2C40: Proves that the diversity of matter is not the first cause of the distinction among things, since matter alone, without an ordering agent, could produce determinate results only by chance.
B2C41: Proves that the distinction among things is not caused by contrariety or diversity among multiple uncoordinated agents, since ordered effects require a single ordering cause behind any cooperating agents.
B2C42: Refutes the view that the order of secondary agents, cascading in decreasing simplicity from God, is the first cause of the world's diversity, showing this fails to assign one true first cause to all diversity.
B2C43: Refutes certain heretics' claim that God created only formless matter which an angel then diversified with various forms, showing this to be impossible especially regarding incorruptible heavenly bodies.
B2C44: Refutes Origen's view that the diversity among creatures results from differing merits and demerits of rational souls that existed and sinned before receiving their present bodily conditions.
B2C45: Explains the true first cause of the distinction among things: God's intent to communicate His own perfect likeness as fully as possible required a diverse multitude of creatures rather than one uniform kind.
B2C46: Argues that the perfection of the universe required the existence of intellectual creatures, since a return of effects to their source, achieved through likeness, brings the universe to its fullest perfection.
B2C49: Continues arguing for the necessity of intellectual creatures, since God's goodness had to be communicated not only through being but through knowledge, which only an intellect can attain.
B2C50: Proves that intellectual substances are immaterial, since bodies are individuated and divided by matter, while the intellect must be free from matter to receive the universal, abstracted forms it understands.
B2C51: Proves that intellectual substances are subsistent forms not dependent on matter for their being, since forms embedded in matter cannot themselves understand, only the composite could, which is impossible for intellect.
B2C52: Proves that in created intellectual substances there remains a real difference between their being and what they are, unlike in God, since only in God are essence and existence identical.
B2C53: Proves that created intellectual substances are composed of act and potentiality, since their substance stands to their received being as potentiality stands to its completing act.
B2C54: Distinguishes the composition of substance and being found in intellectual substances from the composition of matter and form found in bodies, showing these are not the same kind of composition.
B2C55: Proves that intellectual substances are incorruptible, since corruption requires separation of form from matter, and intellectual substances, lacking matter, admit of no such separation.
B2C56: Begins inquiring how an intellectual substance can be united to a body, first ruling out union by mixture, since intellectual substances share no matter in common with bodies to be mixed with.
B2C57: Presents and critiques Plato's opinion that the intellectual soul is united to the body only as a mover to what is moved, like a sailor in a ship, rather than as a substantial form.
B2C59: Presents the opinion, attributed to Averroes, that the possible intellect Aristotle describes is a separate substance, not truly united to the human being as its form.
B2C60: Explains Averroes's position that man's specific difference from brutes comes not from the separate possible intellect but from the cogitative power, identified loosely with a kind of passive intellect.
B2C61: Argues against Averroes by showing that his interpretation of the possible intellect as a separate substance is actually contrary to Aristotle's own text and teaching on the soul.
B2C62: Presents and critiques Alexander of Aphrodisias's opinion that the possible intellect is merely a power resulting from the bodily mixture of elements in man, not itself an intellectual substance.
B2C64: Refutes the theory, attributed to Empedocles and Dinarchus, that the soul is merely a harmony or temperament of the body's contrary elements, since harmony cannot rule or move a body as the soul does.
B2C65: Refutes the ancient materialist view that the soul is itself a body, since living things are composed of matter and form, and the soul, as the form making them alive, cannot itself be a body.
B2C66: Refutes the early philosophers who identified intellect with sense perception, showing that intellect grasps universals while sense knows only particulars, so the two powers must be really distinct.
B2C69: Resolves the earlier arguments claiming an intellectual substance cannot be united to a body as its form, showing that body and soul together form one actually existing substance rather than two.
B2C70: Argues, based on Aristotle's proof of a first self-moving mover composed of moving and moved parts, that Aristotle's own principles require the intellect to be united to the body as its form.
B2C71: Proves that the soul is united to the body immediately, without any intermediary such as phantasms, powers, or a corporeal spirit, since form is united to matter directly by its very nature.
B2C72: Proves that the whole soul is present in the whole body and in each of its parts, since it is the substantial form of the entire organic body and of every part composing it.
B2C74: Presents Avicenna's opinion that intelligible forms are not permanently retained in the possible intellect but exist there only while actually being understood, requiring renewed abstraction each time.
B2C75: Refutes the arguments used to prove there is only one possible intellect shared by all humans, addressing the claim that a form multiplied in matter must be individuated by that matter.
B2C76: Proves that the active intellect, like the possible intellect, is not a separate substance shared by all but a proper part of each individual human soul.
B2C77: Shows it is not impossible for the possible and active intellect to be powers of one and the same soul, since a thing can be potential in one respect and actual in another simultaneously.
B2C79: Proves that the human soul is not corrupted when the body is corrupted, since it is an incorruptible intellectual substance whose perfection consists precisely in a certain abstraction from the body.
B2C80: Presents arguments claiming the soul must be corrupted along with the body, based on the multiplication of souls according to bodies and the specific unity that would seem to require after death.
B2C81: Continues presenting arguments for the soul's corruption with the body, exploring further difficulties concerning the multiplicity and individuation of surviving souls after bodily death.
B2C84: Solves earlier arguments claiming souls existed before their bodies, clarifying that a power to exist always concerns the future, not the past, so it does not imply pre-existence.
B2C85: Proves that the human soul is not made of God's own substance, since God is eternal and unchangeable while the soul begins to exist, and God cannot be the form of anything.
B2C86: Proves that the human soul is not transmitted through the semen in generation, since operations independent of bodily organs, like intellection, cannot arise from a merely bodily generative process.
B2C87: Proves that the human soul is brought into being directly through creation by God, since it is neither generated per se nor accidentally, being immaterial and having a genuine beginning of existence.
B2C89: Explains the order and process of human and animal generation, refuting the view that early vital operations in the embryo proceed from the mother's soul rather than the developing being's own.
B2C90: Proves that an intellectual substance is united as form to no body other than the human body, since no other elemental or mixed body could provide the balanced disposition required for such union.
B2C91: Proves that some intellectual substances exist entirely without being united to any body, since surviving human souls, and especially any substance shared by all, must subsist apart from matter.
B2C92: Discusses Aristotle's view on the number of separate substances, arguing they correspond to the number of distinct celestial movements observed in the heavens.
B2C94: Proves that separate substances and the human soul do not belong to the same species, since their proper mode of being differs, the soul alone being naturally united to a body as its form.
B2C95: Explains how genus and species can be attributed to separate substances despite their lacking matter and form, since their degrees of participation in being replace the material/formal distinction found in bodies.
B2C96: Proves that separate substances do not derive their intellectual knowledge from sensible things, since they have no bodily organs and their higher intellectual power requires a correspondingly higher object.
B2C97: Proves that the intellect of a separate substance is always actually understanding, never merely potential, since such substances transcend time and, as living substances, exercise their proper operation continuously.
B2C99: Proves that separate substances know material things through their own intelligible forms, since their perfect intellects comprehend intelligible being in every respect, including the natures of bodies.
B2C100: Proves that separate substances know singular material things and not merely their universal natures, since the more universal and powerful images in their intellects can extend even to individuating conditions.
B2C101: Considers whether separate substances understand all things simultaneously by their natural knowledge, or whether, despite possessing many intelligible species at once, they actually attend to them successively by will.
